topic: MIT 6.824 selected lectures: Raft, linearizability, transactions
track: F. Distributed Systems and System Design
why: Every customer environment you land in already runs consensus somewhere you did not choose: etcd under their Kubernetes control plane, ZooKeeper or KRaft under their Kafka, a MongoDB replica set, a Consul cluster, a CockroachDB or Spanner tier. When the platform team asks 'is it safe if we lose one node', 'why did the API server time out for 40 seconds', or 'why did two workers both think they held the lock', the FDE in the room has to answer from mechanism, not folklore, and then translate the answer into a flag change, a topology change, or a redesign of the customer's retry logic. The same vocabulary (quorum, commit, linearizable, stale read, blocking 2PC, idempotency across failover) is exactly what a Palantir, Databricks or Anthropic system-design loop probes, so the whiteboard fluency this topic builds is doing double duty.
prerequisites: Topic 39 (DDIA and Kleppmann lectures): chapters 5 (replication), 7 (transactions) and 9 (consistency and consensus) read, so terms like quorum, leader-based replication, snapshot isolation and total order broadcast are already familiar

Topic 2 (Networking): what a partition really looks like on the wire (dropped or delayed packets, asymmetric reachability, a slow link that is not down), TCP retransmit and connection timeouts, and why 'the node is unreachable' is indistinguishable from 'the node is slow'
Topic 29 (PostgreSQL at depth): MVCC, READ COMMITTED vs REPEATABLE READ vs SERIALIZABLE, row locks, and what a transaction ID and xmin horizon are
Topic 1 (Linux internals): fsync/fdatasync semantics, why a write is not durable until the flush returns, and roughly what a flush costs on local NVMe vs a network block device
Topic 33 (Kafka): ISR, acks and min.insync.replicas, so the contrast between Kafka's data-plane replication and Raft-style consensus lands
Can read Go at the level of the Raft paper's pseudocode and the etcd/raft or hashicorp/raft README; the 6.824 lectures and the optional lab (Topic 41) assume it

subtopics.name: Replicated state machines, split brain and why majorities
subtopics.learn: State the problem Raft solves: N servers each applying the same deterministic log in the same order so that any one can take over, under a crash-stop plus network-partition failure model (no Byzantine nodes, unbounded message delay, clocks not trusted for safety). Be able to show on a whiteboard why a naive primary-backup with a single 'view server' can split-brain when the network partitions, and why requiring a majority of 2f+1 servers for every decision guarantees any two decisions share at least one server and hence carry the other's history. Know the practical consequences: 3 nodes tolerate 1 failure, 5 tolerate 2, 4 tolerate the same as 3 but is slower, and an even-sized cluster is never a good trade. This is 6.824 lecture 'Fault Tolerance: Raft (1)' and section 5 of the paper.

resource.label: MIT 6.824 schedule (lecture videos and notes for Raft 1 and 2)

subtopics.name: Terms, elections and the election restriction
subtopics.learn: Walk the state machine follower -> candidate -> leader with the exact RequestVote fields (term, candidateId, lastLogIndex, lastLogTerm) and reply (term, voteGranted), and be able to say what a server does on receiving any RPC with a higher term (adopt it, become follower, reset votedFor) or lower term (reject). Explain why election timeouts are randomised (paper uses 150-300 ms; etcd defaults heartbeat 100 ms / election 1000 ms), how a split vote resolves, and the requirement broadcastTime << electionTimeout << MTBF. Nail the election restriction: a voter grants only if the candidate's log is at least as up to date, comparing lastLogTerm first and lastLogIndex second, and be able to argue why this alone is what makes Leader Completeness hold. Step through the visualisation until you can predict every transition before clicking.

resource.label: The Secret Lives of Data - Raft interactive walkthrough

subtopics.name: AppendEntries, the consistency check and log repair
subtopics.learn: Know the AppendEntries fields (term, leaderId, prevLogIndex, prevLogTerm, entries[], leaderCommit) and the follower's algorithm: reject if the entry at prevLogIndex does not have prevLogTerm, otherwise delete any conflicting suffix and append. Explain the leader's per-follower nextIndex (initialised to lastLogIndex+1) and matchIndex (initialised to 0), how a rejection decrements nextIndex and retries, and the fast-backup optimisation from the 6.824 notes where the follower returns the conflicting term and the first index of that term (XTerm/XIndex/XLen) so the leader skips a whole term per round trip. Work every case of Figure 7 (a-f) by hand: for each follower, say what prevLogIndex the leader will settle on and which entries get truncated. Be able to state the Log Matching property and why a follower may never keep an entry the leader does not have.

resource.label: Raft extended paper (6.824 copy) - sections 5.3 and Figure 7

subtopics.name: Commitment, Figure 8 and the five safety properties
subtopics.learn: Define commit precisely: the leader advances commitIndex to N only when a majority have matchIndex >= N and log[N].term == currentTerm; followers learn it via leaderCommit and apply entries up to it. Reproduce Figure 8 on a whiteboard from memory: a leader in term 2 replicates index 2 to a majority, crashes, a term-3 leader with a different index-2 entry overwrites it later, so counting replicas of a prior-term entry would have 'committed' something that gets deleted; hence prior-term entries are only committed indirectly when a current-term entry above them commits, which is why real implementations append a no-op entry on election. Recite and justify Election Safety, Leader Append-Only, Log Matching, Leader Completeness and State Machine Safety, and be able to say which mechanism enforces each.

resource.label: In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm (Raft paper, Figure 8 and section 5.4)

subtopics.name: Figure 2 as an executable spec: what is persistent and when to fsync
subtopics.learn: Classify every variable in Figure 2: persistent (currentTerm, votedFor, log[]) versus volatile (commitIndex, lastApplied, and on leaders nextIndex[], matchIndex[]) and be able to explain the bug that appears if each persistent one is lost (two votes in one term, forgetting a granted vote, resurrecting a deleted entry). Know that persistence means fsync before replying to the RPC, which is why every Raft deployment's latency floor is the WAL fsync and why etcd exposes etcd_disk_wal_fsync_duration_seconds. Read the TLA+ spec alongside Figure 2 and map each action (Timeout, RequestVote, AppendEntries, BecomeLeader, ClientRequest, AdvanceCommitIndex) to the paper's rules; noticing that the spec has no clocks and no timeouts as safety inputs is the point.

resource.label: ongardie/raft.tla - formal TLA+ specification of Raft

subtopics.name: Snapshots and log compaction
subtopics.learn: Explain why an unbounded log is fatal (restart replays forever, disk fills) and how snapshotting works: the service serialises its state at some applied index, Raft discards the log prefix and remembers lastIncludedIndex and lastIncludedTerm so the consistency check still works for the next AppendEntries; lagging followers receive InstallSnapshot (lastIncludedIndex, lastIncludedTerm, offset, data, done). In etcd terms: --snapshot-count (default 100000 entries) triggers a Raft snapshot, --max-snapshots and --max-wals (default 5 each) bound retention, while the separate MVCC history is bounded by --auto-compaction-mode=periodic|revision and --auto-compaction-retention plus etcdctl defrag to reclaim file space. Know that hitting --quota-backend-bytes (default 2 GiB, hard cap 8 GiB) raises the NOSPACE alarm and makes the cluster read-only until you compact, defrag and etcdctl alarm disarm.

resource.label: etcd v3.5 operations guide - Maintenance (compaction, defragmentation, space quota, snapshots)

subtopics.name: Membership changes, learners and the quorum arithmetic trap
subtopics.learn: Explain why a naive switch from C_old to C_new can elect two leaders, and the two fixes: the paper's joint consensus (C_old,new) and the dissertation's simpler single-server-at-a-time change where any two adjacent configurations overlap in a majority. Know the operational hazards that follow: adding a fourth member to a 3-node cluster that already has one dead member drops you from quorum 2-of-3 with 2 healthy to quorum 3-of-4 with 2 healthy, an outage, which is why etcd enforces --strict-reconfig-check and why the rule is remove-then-add. Use etcdctl member add <name> --peer-urls=... --learner then etcdctl member promote so the new node catches up without counting toward quorum, and know that removing the current leader triggers a fresh election you should schedule for a quiet window.

resource.label: etcd v3.5 operations guide - Runtime reconfiguration

subtopics.name: Linearizability: definition and checking a history by hand
subtopics.learn: State the definition operationally: a history is linearizable if you can assign each operation a single point between its invocation and response such that the sequence of points is a legal sequential history of the object. Practise the 6.824 lecture method: draw the invocation/response intervals for concurrent reads and writes to one register, try to place the points, and either produce the order or exhibit the cycle that proves there is none (a read returning a value whose write started after the read completed, or two reads observing writes in opposite orders). Contrast with sequential consistency (no real-time constraint) and eventual consistency, and be able to say in one sentence why linearizability is the model that lets you ignore replication: it behaves like a single copy.

resource.label: Jepsen - Linearizability (consistency models reference)

subtopics.name: Linearizable vs stale reads: ReadIndex, leader leases and the deposed-leader problem
subtopics.learn: Explain why a Raft leader cannot simply answer reads from local state: it may have been deposed by a partition and be serving values a new leader has already overwritten. Know the two remedies: ReadIndex (record commitIndex, confirm leadership with a heartbeat round to a majority, wait until lastApplied >= that index, then serve) and lease-based reads (serve within a lease shorter than the election timeout, which trades a clock-drift assumption for a network round trip). Map this to etcd: etcdctl get --consistency=l (default, ReadIndex) vs --consistency=s (serializable, served locally by any member, may be stale), and know which one your customer's Kubernetes clients and any custom config loaders are actually using. Know what etcd guarantees for a linearizable read after a linearizable write from another client, and what 'serializable' means in etcd's vocabulary versus SQL's.

resource.label: etcd v3.5 - API guarantees (linearizability, serializable reads, revisions)

subtopics.name: Client sessions, duplicate detection and exactly-once semantics
subtopics.learn: Work through the failure: client sends Put, leader commits it, leader crashes before replying, client retries to the new leader, the Put executes twice. Know the standard fix from Raft dissertation chapter 6: each client registers a session ID, tags requests with a monotonically increasing sequence number, and the state machine (not the Raft layer) keeps a per-client table of last-applied sequence and cached reply so a duplicate returns the cached result without re-executing; the table must live in the replicated state so it survives failover, and it needs an expiry policy the cluster agrees on. Translate this to FDE work: an idempotency key column plus unique index in Postgres, or a Redis SETNX with TTL (Topic 31), is the same idea and has the same expiry problem.

resource.label: Diego Ongaro - Consensus: Bridging Theory and Practice (Raft dissertation, ch. 6 client interaction)

subtopics.name: ZooKeeper's weaker model: linearizable writes, FIFO client order, watches
subtopics.learn: Understand why ZooKeeper deliberately serves reads from any replica (throughput scales with followers) and what it promises instead of full linearizability: writes are linearizable and totally ordered by zxid, each client's operations execute in the order it issued them, and a read after your own write sees that write; a client that needs a fresh read calls sync() first. Know the primitives that make it a coordination service rather than a database: ephemeral znodes tied to the session (so a crashed lock holder releases the lock), sequential znodes for fair locks, one-shot watches, and the herd-effect fix of watching only your predecessor. Be able to describe the 'ready znode' pattern for atomic multi-key config updates and why it depends on FIFO client order.

resource.label: ZooKeeper Programmer's Guide - consistency guarantees, watches, znodes

subtopics.name: Timeouts, disks and leader flapping in a real etcd cluster
subtopics.learn: Diagnose the most common customer-cluster pathology: leader elections every few minutes with kube-apiserver logging 'etcdserver: request timed out'. Know the causal chain (slow fsync or network delays heartbeats -> followers time out -> election -> writes stall) and the metrics that separate the causes: etcd_disk_wal_fsync_duration_seconds p99 should be under 10 ms and etcd_disk_backend_commit_duration_seconds under 25 ms, etcd_network_peer_round_trip_time_seconds for network, etcd_server_leader_changes_seen_total for the symptom, plus log lines 'failed to send out heartbeat on time' and 'apply request took too long'. Know the tuning levers and their limits: --heartbeat-interval should be near the peer RTT, --election-timeout about 10x heartbeat and never above 50000 ms, etcd on its own disk (never a shared network volume behind a busy database), and etcdctl check perf to baseline before and after.

resource.label: etcd v3.5 - Tuning (heartbeat, election timeout, disk and network)

subtopics.name: Quorum loss and disaster recovery
subtopics.learn: Enumerate etcd's failure classes (minority loss: fine, elect if needed; leader loss: election within one election timeout; majority loss: read-only at best and unrecoverable without operator action) and know which one the customer is in from etcdctl endpoint status -w table and etcdctl endpoint health. Practise the recovery path: regular etcdctl snapshot save, then etcdutl snapshot restore <file> --name <m> --initial-cluster ... --initial-cluster-token ... --initial-advertise-peer-urls ... --data-dir <new>, which rewrites member and cluster IDs so the old members cannot rejoin, and understand that everything after the snapshot is lost. Know --force-new-cluster as the single-surviving-member last resort and why it is dangerous if another old member later comes back. Tie this to Topic 24 (HA and DR): the RPO for a Kubernetes control plane is your etcd snapshot cadence.

resource.label: etcd v3.5 operations guide - Disaster recovery

subtopics.name: Testing consistency: Porcupine, Jepsen and fault injection
subtopics.learn: Learn how a linearizability checker works so you can use one on a customer system: record every operation's invocation time, response time, inputs and outputs, define a sequential model (a register or key-value map with a step function), and let the checker search for a valid ordering; Porcupine is the Go checker the 6.824 labs use, Knossos and Elle are Jepsen's. Read one Jepsen analysis end to end (jepsen.io/analyses) and identify the nemesis used (partition, clock skew, process kill, pause), the claimed model, and the minimal history that violated it. Know the fault-injection toolkit you can run on a customer's staging cluster: docker pause or kill -STOP for stop-the-world, iptables DROP or docker network disconnect for partitions, tc netem for latency, and why a paused process is worse than a dead one.

resource.label: anishathalye/porcupine - linearizability checker used by the 6.824 labs

subtopics.name: Two-phase commit and why it blocks
subtopics.learn: Draw 2PC precisely: coordinator sends PREPARE, each participant writes a prepare record (locks held, must survive crash) and votes, coordinator durably logs the decision then sends COMMIT/ABORT, participants ack. Identify the blocking window: participants that voted yes cannot unilaterally decide if the coordinator is unreachable, so they hold locks until it returns; contrast with Raft/Paxos where the decision is replicated and a new leader can finish it (Spanner's trick is to make the coordinator itself a Paxos group). Practise the Postgres mechanics: PREPARE TRANSACTION 'gid', COMMIT PREPARED / ROLLBACK PREPARED, max_prepared_transactions (default 0, i.e. disabled), and the pg_prepared_xacts view, and know that an orphaned prepared transaction is invisible in pg_stat_activity yet holds its row locks and pins the xmin horizon so VACUUM cannot advance.

resource.label: PostgreSQL docs - PREPARE TRANSACTION

subtopics.name: Spanner: TrueTime, commit-wait and external consistency
subtopics.learn: Explain Spanner's architecture in FDE terms: data split into tablets, each replicated by its own Paxos group across zones, read-write transactions use 2PL for locks and 2PC across groups with a Paxos-replicated coordinator, and timestamps come from TrueTime, an API returning an interval [earliest, latest] bounded by GPS and atomic clocks. Nail commit-wait: a transaction is assigned timestamp s = TT.now().latest and the leader waits until TT.after(s) before releasing locks, so any transaction that starts after this one returns is guaranteed a larger timestamp, which yields external consistency (strict serializability); remove commit-wait and a later transaction could get an earlier timestamp and read-only transactions would observe an impossible order. Know why read-only transactions are lock-free (pick a timestamp, read the snapshot from any sufficiently up-to-date replica) and how Cloud Spanner exposes strong, bounded-staleness (max_staleness, min_read_timestamp) and exact-staleness (exact_staleness, read_timestamp) reads.

resource.label: Cloud Spanner docs - TrueTime and external consistency

subtopics.name: Isolation levels versus consistency models
subtopics.learn: Separate two axes that customers conflate: consistency models (linearizability) are about single operations on single objects across replicas and real time, while isolation levels (serializability) are about multi-object transactions on one logical database and say nothing about real time; strict serializability is both. Be able to give the classic anomaly per level with Postgres specifics: READ COMMITTED (default) allows non-repeatable reads, REPEATABLE READ is snapshot isolation and allows write skew (two doctors both going off-call), SERIALIZABLE uses SSI and aborts with SQLSTATE 40001 'could not serialize access', so every caller needs a retry loop. Then give the cross-system example: a Raft-backed key-value store is linearizable per key but not transactional across keys, and a single-node Postgres at SERIALIZABLE is serializable but its async read replica is neither.

resource.label: PostgreSQL docs - Transaction Isolation

subtopics.name: Leases and fencing: leader election without owning a consensus library
subtopics.learn: Understand how Kubernetes components elect a leader without implementing Raft themselves: a coordination.k8s.io/v1 Lease object with holderIdentity, leaseDurationSeconds, acquireTime, renewTime and leaseTransitions, updated with optimistic concurrency against etcd (which is the actual consensus); client-go's defaults are LeaseDuration 15 s, RenewDeadline 10 s, RetryPeriod 2 s, and kube-controller-manager exposes them as --leader-elect-lease-duration and friends. Be able to explain why a lease is not a fence: a holder paused by GC or the hypervisor for longer than the lease can resume and act after a new holder exists, so any external side effect must carry a fencing token (etcd revision, ZooKeeper zxid, or a monotonically increasing epoch column) that the downstream store rejects if it is lower than the last one seen. Apply the same reasoning to any customer 'distributed lock' built on Redis SET NX PX.

resource.label: Kubernetes docs - Leases (coordination.k8s.io)

subtopics.name: Consensus in the systems you will inherit: KRaft, MongoDB, CockroachDB
subtopics.learn: Build the Rosetta stone you will use on site. Kafka: KRaft replaces ZooKeeper with a Raft-style controller quorum (process.roles, controller.quorum.voters or the dynamic controller.quorum.bootstrap.servers, the __cluster_metadata log) that is pull-based rather than push-based, while data partitions still use ISR replication where durability depends on acks=all, min.insync.replicas>=2 and unclean.leader.election.enable=false, not on Raft. MongoDB: replica-set elections with electionTimeoutMillis (default 10000 ms) and member priority, writeConcern w:majority to avoid rollback of acknowledged writes after failover, readConcern majority vs linearizable (primary only, re-confirms leadership). CockroachDB: each range (default 512 MiB) is its own Raft group, a leaseholder serves reads without a Raft round, and clock uncertainty (--max-offset, default 500 ms) is handled with hybrid logical clocks instead of TrueTime. For each, be able to state what 'lost one node' and 'lost a majority' mean operationally.

resource.label: Apache Kafka documentation - KRaft (section 6.9 and replication design)

subtopics.name: Whiteboard rehearsal: the 15-minute Raft explanation
subtopics.learn: Script and rehearse the deliverable: (1) the problem and the majority argument, (2) normal-case election with RPC fields and randomised timeouts, (3) normal-case replication with prevLogIndex/prevLogTerm and commit, (4) a leader failure with a Figure 7-style divergence and the repair, (5) the Figure 8 trap and the current-term commit rule, (6) a one-minute coda on persistence, snapshots and linearizable reads. Use RaftScope on raft.github.io to stage each scenario, pause it, and practise narrating the exact state on screen without reading it, then redo the same scenario on a blank whiteboard. Time yourself; if any segment exceeds its budget, cut detail rather than speed up, because the interviewer will interrupt at the point they care about.

resource.label: raft.github.io - Raft homepage with RaftScope interactive visualisation

outcomes: You can draw a 5-node Raft cluster on a whiteboard and narrate election, replication and commit with the correct RPC fields and persistence points, including the Figure 8 case, in under 15 minutes with no notes and survive interruptions at any step

You can take any Figure 7-style log configuration and state, per server, whether it can win an election, what prevLogIndex the leader will settle on for each follower, and which entries will be truncated
You can decide by hand whether a short history of concurrent reads and writes is linearizable, and confirm it by feeding the same history to Porcupine with a register model

You can look at etcd metrics and logs from a customer cluster and attribute leader flapping to fsync latency, network RTT or misconfigured timeouts, naming the exact flag or infrastructure change that fixes it
You can explain when two-phase commit blocks, list orphaned prepared transactions in Postgres from pg_prepared_xacts, and articulate why Spanner's Paxos-replicated coordinator does not block
You can explain commit-wait and external consistency to a non-Google engineer and translate it into what a customer should expect from Cloud Spanner's strong versus stale reads

You can map the words quorum, leader, commit, linearizable and stale to their concrete equivalents in Kafka KRaft, MongoDB replica sets, CockroachDB ranges and Kubernetes Leases in a live customer conversation
You can spot an unsafe distributed lock or leader lease in a customer's code and propose a fencing-token design with a specific token source and enforcement point
failureModes: etcd placed on a shared network volume alongside a busy database: WAL fsync p99 climbs past 10 ms, heartbeats are late, the cluster elects a new leader every few minutes and kube-apiserver returns 'etcdserver: request timed out' across the whole platform

Operator 'fixes' a 3-node cluster with one dead member by adding a replacement before removing the dead one: quorum goes from 2-of-3 to 3-of-4 with only 2 healthy, and the control plane goes read-only mid-incident

A config or leader-election loader reads etcd with --consistency=s (or ZooKeeper without sync()) and occasionally acts on a value the customer overwrote seconds earlier, producing two workers that both believe they own a shard

A JVM app using XA against Postgres crashes between PREPARE and COMMIT; the orphaned prepared transaction never shows up in pg_stat_activity but holds row locks for days and pins the xmin horizon until autovacuum warnings about wraparound appear
A client library retries a write after a leader change with no idempotency key, so the payment or Kafka publish executes twice; the team blames the database for 'duplicating data'

Kafka producers run with acks=1 or min.insync.replicas=1 plus unclean.leader.election.enable=true; a broker failover silently discards acknowledged messages and the customer's audit reconciliation fails weeks later

A worker holding a Redis or Lease-based lock is paused by a stop-the-world GC longer than the TTL, another worker acquires the lock, and both write to the downstream store because nothing checked a fencing token
interviewQuestions: Whiteboard this: a 5-node Raft cluster, the term-3 leader has replicated index 7 to two followers and then crashes. Walk through the possible elections that follow, state in each case what happens to index 7, and explain precisely why Raft refuses to count replicas of prior-term entries when advancing commitIndex.

A customer's 3-node etcd cluster under Kubernetes shows a leader change every few minutes and intermittent API server timeouts. What do you check, in what order, what metrics and log lines do you expect to see for each hypothesis, and what would you change first?

Explain the difference between linearizability, serializability and strict serializability with one concrete anomaly each. Name a production system that is serializable but not linearizable and describe the customer-visible symptom.

A service reads its shard assignment from etcd using serializable reads and a customer reports that after a rebalance two instances occasionally process the same shard for a few seconds. Explain the mechanism and propose three fixes with their latency and availability trade-offs.

Design exactly-once processing for inbound webhooks in a service that runs three replicas behind a load balancer and restarts during deploys. Where does the deduplication state live, how does it survive failover, and how do you expire it without reintroducing duplicates?
Why does Spanner make committing transactions wait, what would break if you removed commit-wait, and how does a system without TrueTime such as CockroachDB approximate the same guarantee?

A customer wants to coordinate two databases with two-phase commit from their application server. Walk through what happens if the application server dies after both participants voted yes, then tell me when you would push back and what you would build instead.
proofOfWork: A public 'stale read lab' repository: a docker-compose file that stands up a 3-member etcd 3.5 cluster plus Prometheus, a small Go or Python driver that runs N concurrent clients issuing put/get against a handful of keys while recording invocation and response timestamps and values, and a fault script that pauses the current leader (docker pause, simulating a stop-the-world) and partitions one member (docker network disconnect) during the run. The driver is run twice, once with reads at --consistency=s and once at --consistency=l, and both histories are fed to Porcupine with a register model; the repository commits the two checker outputs (the serializable run fails with the minimal violating sub-history highlighted, the linearizable run passes), Grafana screenshots of etcd_server_leader_changes_seen_total and etcd_disk_wal_fsync_duration_seconds across the fault window, and a one-page README that names the exact Raft mechanism (ReadIndex) responsible for the difference, what the same misconfiguration looks like in a customer's Kubernetes or ZooKeeper setup, and the flag or code change an operator should make. As a bonus, include annotated RaftScope screenshots reproducing the Figure 8 scenario step by step.
